title: Prepositions
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Prepositions of time, place and direction, and fixed word-preposition pairs

introduction.overview: A preposition is a word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence, such as time (at 6 a.m., on Monday, in 1999), place (on the table, in the room), direction (to the market, from Delhi) and many other connections. Many prepositions are fixed with particular words: good at, afraid of, married to, prefer to. These fixed pairs, rather than rules, are the main focus of prepositions questions in placement tests.
introduction.placementRelevance: Preposition fill-in-the-blank items are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds and in error-spotting passages.
introduction.realWorldContext: Using the wrong preposition in an email ("discuss about", "married with") is a common error that makes writing look careless.

learningObjectives: Use at, on and in correctly with time and place
Use since and for correctly with perfect tenses
Memorise common adjective + preposition and verb + preposition pairs
Avoid unnecessary prepositions (discuss about, enter into a room)

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A preposition is always followed by a noun, pronoun or an -ing form (the object of the preposition). If a pronoun follows, it takes the object form (with him, for them).

coreDefinitions: Preposition of time: shows when (at 6 a.m., on Monday, in 1999, since 2018, for five years, by Friday, before and after).
Preposition of place: shows where (in the room, on the table, at the door, under the bridge, near the park).
Preposition of direction: shows movement (to the market, from Delhi, into the room, across the road).
Dependent preposition: a preposition that goes with a particular adjective, noun or verb (afraid of, good at, depend on).
Object of a preposition: the noun, pronoun or -ing word that follows the preposition.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Prepositions are small but they behave like glue: the right one is decided by habit and convention rather than logic. The best approach is to learn them in pairs, as chunks (fond of, interested in, married to), and to apply a few simple rules for time and place.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: For time, think of a funnel: at for exact points (at 6 a.m.), on for days and dates (on Monday), in for longer periods (in July, in 1999). For place the same pattern holds: at for a point (at the door), on for a surface (on the table), in for an enclosed space (in the room).

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: At / on / in (time)
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: at + clock time or point;  on + day or date;  in + month, year, season, part of day
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: at 6 a.m., on Monday, in 1999, in the morning

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: At / on / in (place)
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: at + point;  on + surface;  in + enclosed area, city, country
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: at the door, on the table, in Delhi

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Since and for
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: since + point of time;  for + length of time

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Between and among
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: between = two items (or a few clearly separate items);  among = more than two, in a group
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: between the two children; among the five children

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Common pairs
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: good at, afraid of, fond of, interested in, married to, senior/junior to, prefer ... to, insist on, angry with (a person) / at (a thing), die of / die in
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: He is good at Mathematics. I prefer tea to coffee.

mainNarrative: Start with the three common prepositions of time. Use at for exact times (at 6 a.m., at noon, at night), on for days and dates (on Monday, on 15 August) and in for months, years, seasons and parts of the day (in July, in 1999, in summer, in the morning).

The same funnel works for place. At marks a point (at the door, at the bus stop), on marks a surface (on the table, on the wall) and in marks an enclosed space or area (in the room, in Delhi, in India). Direction words show movement: to (towards a place), from (the starting point), into (entering).

Since and for are often confused. Use since with a point of time (since 2018, since morning) and for with a length of time (for five years, for two hours). Both usually go with perfect tenses: She has been working here since 2018 / for five years.
Between is used for two items; among for more than two items considered as a group. "The teacher divided the sweets between the two children"; "The sweets were distributed among the five children".

Many adjectives and verbs take fixed prepositions: good at, fond of, afraid of, interested in, married to, senior to, prefer X to Y, insist on, accuse of, die of. Do not use extra prepositions: say "discuss the matter" (not "discuss about"), "enter the room" (not "enter into the room").

deepDiveAspects.title: Angry with or at
deepDiveAspects.content: We are angry with a person and angry at something a person did: She is angry with me for being late; She is angry at the delay.

deepDiveAspects.title: Prefer to, not than
deepDiveAspects.content: The verb prefer is followed by to, not than: I prefer tea to coffee. Similarly, senior and junior take to: He is senior to me.

problemVariations.exampleSnippet: She has worked here ___ five years.
The sweets were divided ___ the five children.

solvedExamples.title: At, on, in for time
solvedExamples.question: Fill in the blanks: (a) She was born ___ 1999. (b) The meeting is ___ Monday. (c) I wake up ___ 6 a.m.
givenInfo: (a) a year, (b) a day, (c) a clock time
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: in for years, on for days, at for clock times.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The funnel runs from the most specific (clock time) to the most general (year).

solvedExamples.title: Since or for
solvedExamples.question: Fill in the blanks with since or for: (a) She has worked here ___ 2018. (b) She has worked here ___ five years.
givenInfo: (a) a point of time, (b) a length of time

steps.title: (a) 2018
steps.explanation: A point of time takes since.

steps.title: (b) five years
steps.explanation: A length of time takes for.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Both sentences say the same thing in different ways.

solvedExamples.title: Between or among
solvedExamples.question: Fill in the blanks: (a) The teacher divided the sweets ___ the two children. (b) The sweets were distributed ___ the five children.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: between for two; among for more than two.

steps.title: (b) five children
steps.explanation: A group of more than two takes among.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Between points to a relationship of two items; among is used for a group.

shortcutMethods.title: Chunk learning

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Learn word + preposition as one chunk (fond of, good at, prefer to, married to) and say the chunk in your head to test the blank. For time and place apply the at-on-in funnel.

rulesForApplication: at → exact point; on → day, date, surface; in → period, enclosed space.
since → point of time; for → length of time.
between → two; among → more than two.
Never add extra prepositions after discuss, enter, reach, attend.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using "since" with a length of time
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Use for with a period and since with a starting point.
The verbs discuss, enter, reach and attend take the object directly.
Learn good at, afraid of, fond of, interested in.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Say each option with the adjacent word as a chunk; the wrong ones usually sound unnatural at once.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Use the idiom lists to revise; prepositions reward repeated reading rather than rules.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Error-spotting items often hide an extra or wrong preposition in a long sentence.

summaryBullets: Common chunks: good at, afraid of, fond of, married to, prefer to.
No extra preposition after discuss, enter, reach.
quickFormulas: at 6 a.m. / on Monday / in July

keyTakeaways: Use the funnel for time and place.
selfCheckQuestions: Can I complete "He is fond ___ music"?
Can I choose between since and for?
Can I fix "He prefers tea than coffee"?
